<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The USEPA issued a
proposed rule&nbsp;on October&nbsp;20, 2005 concerning the test for measuring
whether modifications to electric generating units should trigger application
of New Source Review (NSR) standards under the CAA.&#160; A supplemental rule&nbsp;was also proposed on
May&nbsp;8, 2007 to include additional options for determining if there is an
emissions increase when an existing electric generating unit makes a physical
or operational change.&#160; The rule&nbsp;was
challenged by environmental organizations and has not been finalized.&#160; While we cannot at this time predict the
outcome of this rulemaking, any finalized rules&nbsp;could materially affect
our operations.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On December&nbsp;17,
2003, the USEPA proposed the Interstate Air Quality Rule&nbsp;(IAQR) designed
to reduce and permanently cap SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and NOx emissions from electric
utilities.&#160; The proposed IAQR focused on
states, including Ohio, whose power plant emissions are believed to be
significantly contributing to fine particle and ozone pollution in other
downwind states in the eastern United States.&#160;
On June&nbsp;10, 2004, the USEPA issued a supplemental proposal to the
IAQR, now renamed the CAIR.&#160; The final rules&nbsp;were
signed on March&nbsp;10, 2005 and were published on May&nbsp;12, 2005.&#160; CAIR created an interstate trading program
for annual NOx emission allowances and made modifications to an existing
trading program for SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160;
On August&nbsp;24, 2005, the USEPA proposed additional revisions to the
CAIR.&#160; On July&nbsp;11, 2008, the U.S.
Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued a decision to
vacate the USEPA&#146;s CAIR and its associated Federal Implementation Plan and
remanded to the USEPA with instructions to issue new regulations that conformed
to the procedural and substantive requirements of the CAA.&#160; The Court&#146;s decision, in part, invalidated
the new NOx annual emission allowance trading program and the modifications to
the SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emission trading program established by the March&nbsp;10,
2005 rules, and created uncertainty regarding future NOx and SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emission
reduction requirements and their timing.&#160;
The USEPA and a group representing utilities filed a request on September&nbsp;24,
2008 for a rehearing before the entire
Court.&nbsp; On December&nbsp;23, 2008, the U.S. Court of Appeals issued
an order on reconsideration that permits CAIR to remain in effect until the
USEPA issues new regulations that would conform to the CAA requirements and the
Court&#146;s July&nbsp;11, 2008 decision.&nbsp; In January&nbsp;2010, the Court
ordered the USEPA to file a response to request for a USEPA decision filed by
parties in the original case who are now seeking a Court order to require the
USEPA to issue new regulations by March&nbsp;1, 2010.&nbsp; We are currently
unable to predict the outcome of this request or the timing or impact of any
new regulations relating to CAIR.&#160; CAIR
has and will continue to have a material effect on our operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In 2007, the Ohio
EPA revised their State Implementation Plan (SIP) to incorporate a CAIR program
consistent with the IAQR.&#160; The Ohio EPA
had received partial approval from the USEPA and had been awaiting full program
approval from the USEPA when the U.S. Court of Appeals issued its July&nbsp;11,
2008 decision.&#160; As a result of the December&nbsp;23,
2008 order, the Ohio EPA proposed revised rules&nbsp;on May&nbsp;11, 2009,
which were finalized on July&nbsp;15, 2009. On September&nbsp;25, 2009, the
USEPA issued a full SIP approval for the Ohio CAIR program.&#160; We do not expect that full SIP approval of
the Ohio CAIR program will have a significant impact on operations.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In the fourth quarter of
2007, <b>DP&amp;L</b> began a program for selling
excess emission allowances, including annual NOx</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">  </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">emission
allowances and SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2 </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">emission allowances that were the subject
of CAIR trading programs.&#160; In subsequent
quarters, <b>DP&amp;L</b> recognized gains from the sale
of excess emission allowances to third parties.&#160;
The court&#146;s CAIR decision affected the trading market for excess
allowances and impacted <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
program for selling additional excess allowances in 2008.&#160; Although in January&nbsp;2009 we resumed
selling excess allowances due to the revival of the trading market, the
long-term impact of the court&#146;s decision and of the actions the USEPA or others
will take in response to this decision,<b>  </b>is not fully
known at this time and could have an adverse effect on us.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On January&nbsp;30,
2004, the USEPA published its proposal to restrict mercury and other air toxins
from coal-fired and oil-fired utility plants.&#160;
The USEPA &#147;de-listed&#148; mercury as a hazardous air pollutant from
coal-fired and oil-fired utility plants and, instead, proposed a cap-and-trade
approach to regulate the total amount of mercury emissions allowed from such
sources.&#160; The final Clean Air Mercury Rule&nbsp;(CAMR)
was signed March&nbsp;15, 2005 and was published on May&nbsp;18, 2005.&#160; On March&nbsp;29, 2005, nine states sued the
USEPA, opposing the cap-and-trade regulatory approach taken by the USEPA.&#160; In 2007, the Ohio EPA adopted rules&nbsp;implementing
the CAMR program.&#160; On February&nbsp;8,
2008, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit struck
down the USEPA regulations, finding that the USEPA had not complied with statutory
requirements applicable to &#147;de-listing&#148; a hazardous air pollutant and that a
cap-and-trade approach was not authorized by law for &#147;listed&#148; hazardous air
pollutants.&#160; A request for rehearing
before the entire Court of Appeals was denied and a petition for review before
the U.S. Supreme Court was filed on October&nbsp;17, 2008.&#160; On February&nbsp;23, 2009, the U.S. Supreme
Court denied the petition.&#160; The USEPA is
expected to move forward on setting Maximum Available Control Technology (MACT)
standards for coal- and oil-fired electric generating units.&#160; Upon publication in the federal register
following finalization, affected exempt generating units (EGUs) will have three
years to come into compliance with the new requirements.&#160; At this time, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is unable to determine the impact of the promulgation of new MACT standards on
its financial position or results of operations; however, a MACT standard could
have a material adverse effect on our operations, in particular, our unscrubbed
units.&#160; We cannot at this time project
the final costs we may incur to comply with any resulting mercury restriction
regulations.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">16<a name="PB_16_002100_8627"></a></font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On January&nbsp;5,
2005, the USEPA published its final non-attainment designations for the
National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for Fine Particulate Matter 2.5
(PM 2.5).&nbsp; These designations included counties and partial counties in
which <b>DP&amp;L</b> operates or owns generating
facilities.&nbsp; On March&nbsp;4, 2005, <b>DP&amp;L</b> and
other Ohio electric utilities and electric generators filed a petition for
review in the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, challenging the final rule&nbsp;creating
these designations.&nbsp; On November&nbsp;30, 2005, the court ordered the
USEPA to decide on all petitions for reconsideration by January&nbsp;20,
2006.&#160; On January&nbsp;20, 2006, the
USEPA denied the petitions for reconsideration.&#160;
On July&nbsp;7, 2009, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the USEPA
non-attainment designations for the areas impacting <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
generation plants, however, on October&nbsp;8, 2009, the USEPA issued new
designations based on 2008 monitoring data that showed all areas in attainment
to the standard with the exception of several counties in northeastern
Ohio.&#160; The USEPA is expected to propose
revisions to the PM 2.5 standard in late 2010 as part of its routine five-year rule&nbsp;review
cycle.&#160; At this time, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is unable to determine the impact the revisions to
the PM 2.5 standard will have on its financial position or results of
operations.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On May&nbsp;5, 2004, the
USEPA issued its proposed regional haze rule, which addresses how states should
determine the Best Available Retrofit Technology (BART) for sources covered
under the regional haze rule.&nbsp; Final rules&nbsp;were published July&nbsp;6,
2005, providing states with several options for determining whether sources in
the state should be subject to BART.&nbsp; In the final rule, the USEPA made
the determination that CAIR achieves greater progress than BART and may be used
by states as a BART substitute.&nbsp; Numerous units owned and operated by us
will be impacted by BART. &nbsp;We cannot determine the extent of the impact
until Ohio determines how BART will be implemented.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In response to a U.S.
Supreme Court decision that the USEPA has the authority to regulate CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emissions from
motor vehicles, the USEPA made a finding that CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and certain other gases are pollutants under
the CAA.&nbsp; The USEPA has not yet identified the specifics of how these
newly designated pollutants will be regulated.&#160;
In April&nbsp;2009, the USEPA issued a proposed endangerment finding
under the CAA.&#160; The proposed finding
determined that CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and other GHGs from motor vehicles threaten
the health and welfare of future generations by contributing to climate
change.&#160; If the proposed finding is
finalized, it could lead to the regulation of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and other GHGs from sources other than motor
vehicles, including coal-fired plants that we own and operate.&#160; Recently, several bills have been introduced
at the federal level to regulate GHG emissions.&#160;
In June&nbsp;2009, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 2454,
the American Clean Energy and Security Act (ACES).&#160; This proposed legislation targets a reduction
in the emission of GHGs from large sources by 80% in 2050 through an
economy-wide cap and trade program.&#160; ACES
also includes energy efficiency and renewable energy initiatives.&#160; Approximately 99% of the energy we produce is
generated by coal.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
share of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emissions at generating stations we own and
co-own is approximately 16 million tons annually.&#160; Proposed GHG legislation finalized at a
future date could have a significant effect on <b>DP&amp;L&#146;</b>s
operations and costs, which could adversely affect our net income, cash flows
and financial position.&#160; However, due to
the uncertainty associated with such legislation, we are currently unable to
predict the final outcome or the financial impact that this legislation will
have on us.&#160; On September&nbsp;22, 2009,
the USEPA issued a final rule&nbsp;for mandatory reporting of GHGs from large
sources that emit 25,000 metric tons per year or more of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">,&#160; including
electric generating units.&#160; The first
report is due in March&nbsp;2011 for 2010 emissions.&#160; This reporting rule&nbsp;will guide
development of policies and programs to reduce emissions.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> does
not anticipate that this reporting rule&nbsp;will result in any significant
cost or other impact on current operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;15, 2009,
the USEPA proposed revisions to its primary NAAQS for nitrogen dioxide.&#160; This change could affect certain emission
sources in heavy traffic areas like the I-75 corridor between Cincinnati and
Dayton.&#160; At this point, <b>DP&amp;L</b> cannot determine the effect of this potential
change, if any, on its operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The USEPA proposed
revisions to its primary NAAQS for SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;on November&nbsp;16, 2009.&#160; This would replace the current 24-hour
standard and current annual standard.&#160;
This regulation is expected to be finalized in 2010.&#160; At this time, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
cannot determine the effect of this potential change, if any, on its
operations.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On September&nbsp;16,
2009, the USEPA announced that it would reconsider the 2008 national ground
level ozone standard.&#160; A more stringent
ambient ozone standard may lead to stricter NOx emission standards in the
future.&#160; At this point, <b>DP&amp;L</b> cannot determine the effect of this potential change,
if any, on its operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Air
Quality &#151; Litigation Involving Co-Owned Plants</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In March&nbsp;2000, as
amended in June&nbsp;2004, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a complaint in
the United States District Court, Southern District of Indiana, Indianapolis
Division against Cinergy Corp. (now part of Duke Energy) and two Cinergy
subsidiaries for alleged violations of the CAA at various generation units
operated by PSI Energy,&nbsp;Inc. and CG&amp;E, including generation units
co-owned by  <b>DP&amp;L</b> (Beckjord Unit 6 and Miami Fort Unit 7).&nbsp;
A retrial has been held in which the second jury found for Duke Energy on some
allegations, but for plaintiffs with respect to units at another one of Duke
Energy&#146;s wholly-owned facilities.&#160; In a
separate phase II remedies trial with respect to violations found in the first
trial, Duke Energy was ordered to close down three of its wholly-owned generating
units by September&nbsp;2009, surrender some emission allowances and pay a
fine.&#160; None of the violations found or
remedies ordered relate to generating units owned in part by <b>DP&amp;L</b>.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In
2004, eight states and the City of New York filed a lawsuit in Federal District
Court for the Southern District of New York against American Electric Power
Company,&nbsp;Inc. (AEP), one of AEP&#146;s subsidiaries, Cinergy Corp. (a
subsidiary of Duke Energy Corporation (Duke Energy)) and four other electric
power companies.&#160; A similar lawsuit was
filed against these companies in the same court by Open Space Institute,&nbsp;Inc.,
Open Space Conservancy,&nbsp;Inc. and The Audubon Society of New
Hampshire.&#160; The lawsuits allege that the
companies&#146; emissions of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;contribute to global warming and constitute a
public or private nuisance.&#160; The lawsuits
seek injunctive relief in the form of specific emission reduction
commitments.&#160; In 2005, the Federal
District Court dismissed the lawsuits, holding that the lawsuits raised
political questions that should not be decided by the courts.&#160; The plaintiffs appealed.&#160; Finding that the plaintiffs have standing to
sue and can assert federal common law nuisance claims, the United States Court
of Appeals for the Second Circuit on September&nbsp;21, 2009 vacated the dismissal
of the Federal District Court and remanded the lawsuits back to the Federal
District Court for further proceedings.&#160;
Although we are not named as a party to these lawsuits, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is a co-owner of coal-fired plants with Duke Energy
and AEP (or their subsidiaries) that could be affected by the outcome of these
lawsuits.&#160; The Second Circuit Court&#146;s
decision could also encourage these or other plaintiffs to file similar
lawsuits against other electric power companies, including us.&#160; We are unable at this time to predict with
certainty the impact that these lawsuits might have on us.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On September&nbsp;21,
2004, the Sierra Club filed a lawsuit against <b>DP&amp;L </b>and
the other owners of the Stuart generating station in the U.S. District Court
for the Southern District of Ohio for alleged violations of the CAA and the
station&#146;s operating permit.&#160; On August&nbsp;7,
2008, a consent decree was filed in the U.S. District Court in full settlement
of these CAA claims.&nbsp; Under the terms of the consent decree, <b>DP&amp;L</b> and the other owners of the Stuart generating
station agreed to: (i)&nbsp;certain emission targets related to NOx, SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and particulate
matter; (ii)&nbsp;make energy efficiency and renewable energy commitments that
are conditioned on receiving PUCO approval for the recovery of costs; (iii)&nbsp;forfeit
5,500 SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;allowances; and (iv)&nbsp;provide funding to a
third party non-profit organization to establish a solar water heater rebate
program.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
and the other owners of the station also entered into an attorneys&#146; fee
agreement to pay a portion of the Sierra Club&#146;s attorney and expert witness
fees.&nbsp; The parties to the lawsuit filed a joint motion on October&nbsp;22,
2008, seeking an order by the U.S. District Court approving the consent decree
with funding for the third party non-profit organization set at $300,000.&#160; On October&nbsp;23, 2008, the U.S. District
Court approved the consent decree.&#160; On October&nbsp;21,
2009, the Sierra Club filed with the U.S. District Court a motion for
enforcement of the consent decree based on the Sierra Club&#146;s interpretation of
the consent decree that would require certain NOx emissions that <b>DP&amp;L</b> has been excluding from its computations to be
included for purposes of complying with the emission targets and reporting
requirements of the consent decree.&nbsp; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
believes that it is properly computing and reporting NOx emissions under the
consent decree and has opposed the Sierra Club&#146;s motion.&#160; A decision on the motion is expected before
the end of the first quarter 2010.&#160;
Because Stuart Station&#146;s NOx emissions are well below the 2009 and 2010
limits in the consent decree under either method of calculation, an adverse
decision would have no effect in 2010 on operations or costs.&#160; An adverse decision could affect compliance
costs in future years when the NOx limits are further reduced under the consent
decree.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Air
Quality &#151; Notices of Violation Involving Co-Owned Plants</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> On March&nbsp;13, 2008, Duke Energy Ohio Inc., the operator of the
Zimmer generating station, received a NOV and a Finding of Violation from the
USEPA alleging violations of the CAA, the Ohio State Implementation Program
(SIP) and permits for the Station in areas including SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">, opacity and increased heat input.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> is a
co-owner of the Zimmer generating station and could be affected by the eventual
resolution of this matter.&#160; Duke Energy
Ohio Inc. is expected to act on behalf of itself and the co-owners with respect
to this matter.&#160; At this time, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is unable to predict the outcome of this matter.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">18<a name="PB_18_002156_3736"></a></font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="left"></div>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">


<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In June&nbsp;2000, the
USEPA issued a NOV to the <b>DP&amp;L</b>-operated
Stuart generating station (co-owned by <b>DP&amp;L</b>,
CG&amp;E and CSP) for alleged violations of the CAA.&#160; The NOV contained allegations consistent with
NOVs and complaints that the USEPA had recently brought against numerous other
coal-fired utilities in the Midwest.&#160; The
NOV indicated the USEPA may: (1)&nbsp;issue an order requiring compliance with
the requirements of the Ohio SIP; or (2)&nbsp;bring a civil action seeking
injunctive relief and civil penalties of up to $27,500 per day for each
violation.&#160; To date, neither action has
been taken.&#160; At this time, <b>DP&amp;L</b> cannot predict the outcome of this matter.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In November&nbsp;1999,
the USEPA filed civil complaints and NOVs against operators and owners of
certain generation facilities for alleged violations of the CAA.&#160; Generation units operated by CG&amp;E
(Beckjord Unit 6) and CSP (Conesville Unit 4) and co-owned by <b>DP&amp;L</b> were referenced in these
actions.&#160; Numerous northeast states have
filed complaints or have indicated that they will be joining the USEPA&#146;s action
against CG&amp;E and CSP.&#160; Although <b>DP&amp;L</b> was not identified in the NOVs,
civil complaints or state actions, the results of such proceedings could
materially affect <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
co-owned plants.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> In December&nbsp;2007, the Ohio EPA issued a NOV to the <b>DP&amp;L</b>-operated Killen generating station (co-owned by <b>DP&amp;L</b> and CG&amp;E) for alleged violations of the
CAA.&#160; The NOVs alleged deficiencies in
the continuous monitoring of opacity.&#160; We
submitted a compliance plan to the Ohio EPA on December&nbsp;19, 2007.&#160; To date, no further actions have been taken
by the Ohio EPA.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Air
Quality &#151; Other Issues Involving Co-Owned Plants</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In 2006, <b>DP&amp;L</b> detected a malfunction with its emission monitoring
system at the <b>DP&amp;L</b>-operated Killen
generating station (co-owned by <b>DP&amp;L</b> and
CG&amp;E) and ultimately determined its SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and NOx emissions data was under
reported.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
has petitioned the USEPA to accept an alternative methodology for calculating
actual emissions for 2005 and the first quarter 2006.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L </b>has
sufficient allowances in its general account to cover the understatement and is
working with the USEPA to resolve the matter.&#160;
Management does not believe the ultimate resolution of this matter will
have a material impact on results of operations, financial position or cash
flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Air
Quality &#151; Notices of Violation Involving Wholly-Owned Plants</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In
2007, the Ohio EPA and the USEPA issued NOVs to <b>DP&amp;L</b>
for alleged violations of the CAA at the O.H. Hutchings Station.&#160; The NOVs alleged deficiencies relate to stack
opacity and particulate emissions.&#160;
Discussions are under way with the USEPA, the U.S. Department of Justice
and Ohio EPA.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
has provided data to those agencies regarding its maintenance expenses and
operating results.&#160; On December&nbsp;15,
2008, <b>DP&amp;L</b> received a request from the
USEPA for additional documentation with respect to those issues and other CAA
issues including issues relating to capital expenses and any changes in
capacity or output of the units at the O.H. Hutchings station.&#160; During
2009, <b>DP&amp;L</b> has continued to
submit various other operational and performance data to the USEPA in compliance
with its request.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L </b>is
currently unable to determine the timing, costs, or method by which the issues
may be resolved and continues to work with the USEPA on this issue.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On November&nbsp;18,
2009, the USEPA issued a NOV to <b>DP&amp;L</b> for
alleged New Source Review (NSR) violations of the CAA at the O.H. Hutchings
Station relating to capital projects performed in 2001 involving Unit 3 and
Unit 6.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
does not believe that the two projects described in the NOV were modifications
subject to NSR.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is unable to determine the timing, costs or method by which these issues may be
resolved and continues to work with the USEPA on this issue.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Water Quality</font></u></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;9,
2004, the USEPA issued final rules&nbsp;pursuant to the Clean Water Act
governing existing facilities that have cooling water intake structures.&nbsp;
The rules&nbsp;require an assessment of impingement or entrainment of organisms
as a result of cooling water withdrawal.&#160;
A number of parties appealed the rules&nbsp;to the Federal Court of
Appeals for the Second Circuit in New York and the Court issued an opinion on January&nbsp;25,
2007 remanding several aspects of the rule&nbsp;to the USEPA for
reconsideration.&nbsp; Several parties petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court for
review of the lower court decision.&#160; On April&nbsp;14,
2008, the Supreme Court elected to review the lower court decision on the issue
of whether the USEPA can compare costs with benefits in determining the best
technology available for minimizing adverse environmental impact at cooling
water intake structures.&#160; Briefs were
submitted to the Court in the summer of 2008 and oral arguments were held in December&nbsp;2008.&#160; In April&nbsp;2009, the U.S. Supreme Court
ruled that the USEPA did have the authority to compare costs with benefits in
determining best technology available.&#160;
The USEPA is developing proposed regulations which it hopes to issue for
public comment by mid-2010.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On May&nbsp;4,
2004, the Ohio EPA issued a final National Pollutant Discharge Elimination
System permit (the Permit) for J.M. Stuart Station that continued our authority
to discharge water from the station into the Ohio River.&#160; During the three-year term of the Permit, we conducted a thermal discharge study
to evaluate the technical feasibility and economic reasonableness of water
cooling methods other than cooling towers.&#160;
In December&nbsp;2006, we submitted an application for the renewal of
the Permit that was due to expire on June&nbsp;30, 2007.&#160; In July&nbsp;2007 we received a draft permit
proposing to continue our authority to discharge water from the station into
the Ohio River. &#160;On February&nbsp;5, 2008
we received a letter from Ohio EPA indicating that they intended to impose a
compliance schedule as part of the final Permit, that requires us to implement
one of two diffuser options for the discharge of water from the station into the
Ohio River as identified in the thermal discharge study.&#160; Subsequently, representatives from <b>DP&amp;L</b> and the Ohio EPA have agreed to allow <b>DP&amp;L</b> to restrict public access to the water discharge
area as an alternative to installing one of the diffuser options.&#160; Ohio EPA issued a revised draft permit that
was received on November&nbsp;12, 2008.&#160;
In December&nbsp;2008, the USEPA requested that the Ohio EPA provide
additional information regarding the thermal discharge in the draft
permit.&#160; In June&nbsp;2009, <b>DP&amp;L</b> provided information to the USEPA in response to
their request to the Ohio EPA.&#160; The
timing for issuance of a final permit is uncertain.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In September&nbsp;2009,
the USEPA announced that it will be revising technology-based regulations
governing water discharges from steam electric generating facilities such as
J.M. Stuart, Killen and O.H. Hutchings Stations.&#160; The rulemaking will include the collection of
information via an industry-wide questionnaire as well as targeted water
sampling efforts at selected facilities.&#160;
Subsequent to the information collection effort, it is anticipated that
the USEPA will release a proposed rule&nbsp;in 2011 with final regulations
issued in late 2012 or early 2013.&#160; At
present, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is unable to predict the
impact this rulemaking will have on its operations.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Land Use and Solid Waste Disposal</font></u></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In September&nbsp;2002, <b>DP&amp;L</b> and other parties received a special notice that the
USEPA considers us to be a PRP for the clean-up of hazardous substances at the
South Dayton Dump landfill site.&#160; In August&nbsp;2005,
<b>DP&amp;L</b> and other parties
received a general notice regarding the performance of a Remedial Investigation
and Feasibility Study (RI/FS) under a Superfund Alternative Approach.&#160; In October&nbsp;2005, <b>DP&amp;L</b> received a special notice letter
inviting it to enter into negotiations with the USEPA to conduct the
RI/FS.&#160; No recent activity has occurred
with respect to that notice or PRP status.&#160;
More recently, <b>DP&amp;L</b> has
received requests by the USEPA and the existing PRP group to allow access to be
given to <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> service center building
site, which is across a street from the landfill site.&#160; The USEPA requested access to drill
monitoring and test wells to determine the extent of the landfill site&#146;s
contamination as well as to assess whether certain chemicals used at the
service center building site might have migrated through groundwater to the
landfill site.&#160; Pursuant to an
Administrative Order issued by the USEPA requiring access to <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> service center building site, <b>DP&amp;L</b> has granted such access and drilling of soil
borings and installation of monitoring wells occurred in the fall of 2009.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L </b>believes
the chemicals used at its service center building site were appropriately
disposed of and have not contributed to the contamination at the South Dayton
Dump landfill site.&#160; While <b>DP&amp;L</b> is unable at this time to predict the outcome of
this matter, if <b>DP&amp;L</b> were required to
contribute to the clean-up of the site, it could have a material adverse effect
on us.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is also unable at this time to predict whether the monitoring and test wells
may lead to any actions relating to the service center building site
independent of the South Dayton Dump clean-up.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In December&nbsp;2003,
<b>DP&amp;L </b>and other parties received a
special notice that the USEPA considers us to be a PRP for the clean-up of hazardous
substances at the Tremont City landfill site.&#160;
Information available to <b>DP&amp;L </b>does
not demonstrate that it contributed hazardous substances to the site.&#160; While <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
unable at this time to predict the outcome of this matter, if <b>DP&amp;L</b> were required to contribute to the clean-up of the
site, it could have a material adverse effect on us.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In November&nbsp;2007,
a PRP group contacted <b>DP&amp;L </b>seeking
our financial participation in a settlement that the group had reached with the
federal government with respect to the clean-up of an industrial site once
owned by Carolina Transformer,&nbsp;Inc.&#160;
<b>DP&amp;L</b>&#146;s business records clearly
show we did not conduct business with Carolina Transformer that would require
our participation in any clean-up of the site.&#160;
<b>DP&amp;L </b>has declined to participate in
the clean-up of this site.&#160; While <b>DP&amp;L</b> is unable at this time to predict the outcome of
this matter, if <b>DP&amp;L</b> were required to
contribute to the clean-up of the site, it could have a material adverse effect
on us.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During
2008, a major spill occurred at an ash pond owned by the Tennessee Valley
Authority (TVA) as a result of a dike failure.&#160;
The spill generated a significant amount of national news coverage, and
support for tighter regulations for the storage and handling of coal combustion
products.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
has ash ponds at the Killen, O.H. Hutchings and J.M. Stuart stations which it
operates, and also at generating stations operated by others but in which <b>DP&amp;L</b> has an ownership interest.&#160; We frequently inspect our ash ponds and do
not anticipate any similar failures.&#160; It
is widely expected that the federal government will propose new regulations
covering ash generated</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">20<a name="PB_20_002453_5335"></a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">from
the combustion of coal including additional monitoring, testing, or
construction standards with respect to ash ponds and ash landfills.&#160; During March&nbsp;2009, the USEPA, through a
formal Information Collection Request, collected information on ash pond
facilities across the country, including those at Killen and J.M. Stuart
stations.&#160; Subsequently the USEPA
collected similar information for O.H. Hutchings Station.&#160; In addition, during August&nbsp;and October&nbsp;2009,
representatives of the USEPA visited J.M. Stuart Station to collect information
on plant operations relative to the production and handling of
by-products.&#160; The USEPA&#146;s contractor has
issued a draft report on their October&nbsp;2009 visit to J.M. Stuart
Station.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
has provided comments on this document and additional related information to
the agency.&#160; Due to the wide range of
possible outcomes, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
unable at this time to predict the timing or the financial impact of any future

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In
addition, as a result of the TVA ash pond spill, there has been increasing
advocacy to regulate coal combustion byproducts as hazardous waste under the
Resource Conservation Recovery Act, Subtitle C.&#160;
On October&nbsp;15, 2009, the USEPA provided a draft rule&nbsp;to the Office
of Management and Budget for interagency review.&#160; The draft rule&nbsp;proposed to regulate coal
ash as a hazardous waste, with limited beneficial reuse.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
unable at this time to predict the financial impact of this regulation, but if
coal combustion byproducts are regulated as hazardous waste, it is expected to
have a material adverse impact on operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Legal and
Other Matters</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In February&nbsp;2007, <b>DP&amp;L</b> filed a lawsuit against a coal supplier seeking
damages incurred due to the supplier&#146;s failure to supply approximately 1.5
million tons of coal to two jointly owned plants under a coal supply agreement,
of which approximately 570 thousand tons was <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
share.&nbsp; <b>DP&amp;L</b> obtained replacement coal
to meet its needs.&#160; The supplier has
denied liability, and is currently in federal bankruptcy proceedings.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
unable to determine the ultimate resolution of this matter at this time.&nbsp;
In accordance with GAAP, <b>DP&amp;L</b> has
not recorded any assets relating to this lawsuit.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On May&nbsp;16, 2007, <b>DPL</b> filed a claim with Energy Insurance
Mutual (EIM) to recoup legal expenses associated with our litigation against
certain former executives.&nbsp; Arbitration on that claim occurred on May&nbsp;13,
2009.&#160; </font><tt><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
arbitration panel issued a ruling in Phase 1 of the arbitration on September&nbsp;25,
2009, finding that most of the claims involving the former executives were
covered.</font></tt><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; The matter is pending.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As a member of PJM, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is also subject to charges and costs associated with PJM operations as approved
by the FERC.&nbsp; FERC Orders issued in 2007 regarding the allocation of costs
of large transmission facilities within PJM, could result in additional costs
being allocated to <b>DP&amp;L </b>of
approximately $12 million or more annually by 2012.&nbsp; <b>DP&amp;L</b> filed a notice of appeal to the
U.S. Court of Appeals, D.C. Circuit on March&nbsp;18, 2008 challenging the
allocation method.&nbsp; The appeal was consolidated with other appeals taken
by other interested parties of the same FERC Orders and the consolidated cases
were assigned to the 7</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">th</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;Circuit.&nbsp; On August&nbsp;6, 2009, the 7</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">th</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;Circuit ruled that the
FERC had failed to provide a reasoned basis for the allocation method it had
approved.&#160; Rehearings were filed by other
interested litigants and denied by the Court, which then remanded the matter to
the FERC for further proceedings.&#160; On January&nbsp;21,
2010, the FERC issued a procedural order on remand establishing a paper hearing
process under which PJM will make an informational filing in late
February.&nbsp; Subsequently PJM and other parties, including <b>DP&amp;L</b>, will be able to file initial comments, testimony,
and recommendations and reply comments.&nbsp; Absent future changes to the
procedural schedule that may occur for a number of reasons including if
settlement discussions are held, the paper hearing process should be complete
and the case ready for FERC consideration in 2010.&nbsp; FERC did not establish
a deadline for its issuance of a substantive order.&nbsp; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
cannot predict the timing or the likely outcome of the proceeding.&#160; Until such time as FERC may act to approve a
change in methodology, PJM will continue to apply the allocation methodology
that had been approved by FERC in 2007.&#160;
Although we continue to maintain that these costs should be borne by the
beneficiaries of these projects and that <b>DP&amp;L</b> is not
one of these beneficiaries, any new credits or additional costs resulting from
the ultimate outcome of this proceeding will be reflected in <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> TCRR rider which is already in place to pass
through RTO-related costs and credits.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In June&nbsp;2009,
the NERC, a FERC-certified electric reliability organization responsible for
developing and enforcing mandatory reliability standards, commenced a routine
audit of <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> operations.&#160; The audit, which was for the period June&nbsp;18,
2007 to June&nbsp;25, 2009, evaluated <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
compliance with 42 requirements in 18 NERC-reliability standards.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
currently subject to a compliance audit at a minimum of once every three years
as provided by the NERC Rules&nbsp;of Procedure. This audit was concluded in June&nbsp;2009
and its findings revealed that <b>DP&amp;L</b> had
some Possible Alleged Violations (PAVs) associated with five NERC Reliability
Standards.&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In response to the
report, <b>DP&amp;L</b> filed mitigation plans with
NERC to address the PAVs.&#160; These
mitigation plans have been accepted and <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
currently awaiting a proposal for settlement from NERC.&#160; While we are currently unable to determine
the extent of penalties, if any, that may be imposed on <b>DP&amp;L</b>,
we do not believe such penalties will have a material impact on our results of
operations.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><b><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Capital
Expenditures for Environmental Matters</font></i></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Test operations of the
FGD equipment on our jointly-owned Conesville Unit 4 were completed in November&nbsp;2009.&#160; The equipment is currently in service.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DPL&#146;s</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> construction additions were approximately
$145 million, $228 million and $347 million in 2009, 2008 and 2007,
respectively, and are expected to approximate $210 million in 2010. &nbsp;</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Planned construction additions for 2010
relate primarily to new investments in and upgrades to <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> power plant equipment and
transmission and distribution system.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DP&amp;L&#146;s</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> construction additions were $144 million, $225
million and $344 million in 2009, 2008 and 2007, respectively, and are expected
to approximate $200 million in 2010.&#160;
Planned construction additions for 2010 relate primarily to new
investments in and upgrades to <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
power plant equipment and transmission and distribution system.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">All
environmental additions made during the past three years pertain to <b>DP&amp;L</b> and approximate $21 million, $90
million and $209 million in 2009, 2008 and 2007, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Item 1A &#151; Risk Factors</font></b><a name="Item1aRiskFactors_002530"></a></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Future operating

operations, financial condition and cash flows could be materially affected.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Regulation and Litigation</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We
are subject to extensive laws and regulation by federal, state and local
authorities, such as the PUCO, the USEPA, the Ohio EPA, the FERC, the SEC and
the Internal Revenue Service, among others. Regulations affect almost every
aspect of our business, including in the areas of the environment, health and
safety, cost recovery and rate making, securities, corporate governance, public
disclosure and reporting and taxation. New laws and regulations, and new
interpretations of existing laws and regulations, are ongoing and we generally
cannot predict the future course of changes in this regulatory environment or
the ultimate effect that this changing regulatory environment will have on our
business.&#160; Complying with this regulatory
environment requires us to expend a significant amount of funds and
resources.&#160; The failure to comply with
this regulatory environment could subject us to substantial financial costs and
penalties and changes, either forced or voluntary, in the way we operate our
business.&#160; Additional detail about the
effect of this regulatory environment on our operations is included in the risk
factors set forth below.</font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In
the normal course of business, we are also subject to various lawsuits,
actions, proceedings, claims and other matters asserted under this regulatory
environment, which require us to expend significant funds to address, the
outcomes of which are uncertain and the adverse resolutions of which could have
a material adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and
cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Cost
Recovery and Rates</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The costs we can recover
and the return on capital we are permitted to earn for certain aspects of our
business are regulated and governed by the laws of Ohio and the rules, policies
and procedures of the PUCO.&#160; On May&nbsp;1,
2008, SB 221, an Ohio electric energy bill, was signed by the Governor of Ohio and
became effective July&nbsp;31, 2008.&#160;
This law, among other things, required all Ohio distribution utilities
to file either an electric security plan or a market rate option that was to be
in effect on January&nbsp;1, 2009, and established a significantly excessive
earnings test for Ohio public utilities based on the earnings of other
companies with similar business and financial risks.&#160; The PUCO approved <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
filed electric security plan on June&nbsp;24, 2009.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
electric security plan provides, among other things, that <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
existing rate plan structure will continue through 2012; that <b>DP&amp;L</b> may seek recovery for adjustments to its existing
rate plan structure for costs associated with storm damage, regulatory and tax
changes, new climate change or carbon regulations, fuel and purchased power and
certain other costs; and that SB 221&#146;s significantly excessive earnings test
will not apply to <b>DP&amp;L</b> until
2012.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
electric security plan, and certain filings made by us in connection with this
plan, are further discussed under &#147;Ohio Retail Rates&#148; in Item 1 &#151; COMPETITION
AND REGULATION.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">While rate regulation is
premised on full recovery of prudently incurred costs and a reasonable rate of
return on invested capital, there can be no assurance that the PUCO will agree
that all of our costs have been prudently incurred or are recoverable or that
the regulatory process in which rates are determined will always result in
rates that will produce a full or timely recovery of our costs and permitted
rates of return.&#160; Certain of our cost
recovery riders are also by-passable by some of our customers.&#160; Accordingly, the rates <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is allowed to charge may or may not match its expenses at any given time.&#160; Therefore, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
could be subject to prevailing market prices for electricity and would not
necessarily be able to charge rates that produce timely or full recovery of its
expenses.&#160; Changes in, or
reinterpretations of, the laws, rules, policies and procedures that set
electric rates and permitted rates of return; changes in <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> ability to recover expenditures
for environmental compliance, reliability initiatives, purchased power and fuel
(which account for a substantial portion of our operating costs), capital
expenditures and investments and other costs on a fully or timely basis through
rates; and changes to the frequency and timing of rate increases could have a
material adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and
cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Advanced Energy and Energy Efficiency Requirements</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">SB 221
contains targets relating to advanced energy, renewable energy, peak demand
reduction and energy efficiency standards.&#160;
The standards require that, by the year 2025 and each thereafter, 25% of
the total number of kWh of electricity sold by the utility to retail electric consumers
must come from alternative energy resources, which include &#147;advanced energy
resources&#148; such as distributed generation, clean coal, advanced nuclear, energy
efficiency and fuel cell technology; and &#147;renewable energy resources&#148; such as
solar, hydro, wind, geothermal and biomass. At least half of the 25% must be
generated from renewable energy resources, including 0.5% from solar energy,
and the remainder must be generated from advanced energy sources. &#160;Annual renewable energy standards began in
2009 with increases in required percentages each year through 2024. The
advanced energy standard must be met by 2025 and each year thereafter.&#160; Annual targets for energy efficiency began in
2009 and require increasing energy reductions each year compared to a baseline
energy usage, up to 22.3% by 2025. Peak demand reduction targets began in 2009
with increases in required percentages each year, up to 7.75% by 2018.&#160; The advanced energy and renewable energy
standards are expected to increase (and could increase materially) our power
supply costs.&#160; Pursuant to <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> approved electric security plan, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is entitled to recover costs associated with its
alternative energy plans, as well as its energy efficiency and demand response
programs, and <b>DP&amp;L</b> began recovering these
costs in 2009.&#160; If in the future we are
unable to timely or fully recover these costs, it could have a material adverse
effect on our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160; In addition, if we were found not to be in
compliance with these standards, monetary penalties could apply.&#160; These penalties are not permitted to be
recovered from customers and significant penalties could have a material
adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and cash
flows.&#160; The demand reduction and energy
efficiency standards by design result in reduced energy and demand that could
adversely affect our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Availability
and Cost of Fuel</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We
purchase coal, natural gas and other fuel from a number of suppliers.&#160; The coal market in particular has experienced
significant price volatility in the last several years.&#160; We are now in a global market for coal in
which our domestic price is increasingly affected by international supply disruptions
and demand balance.&#160; Coal exports from
the U.S. have increased significantly in recent years.&#160; In addition, domestic issues like
government-imposed direct costs and permitting issues that affect mining costs
and supply availability, the variable demand of retail customer load and the
variable performance of our generation fleet have an impact on our fuel
procurement operations.&#160; Our approach is
to hedge the fuel costs for our anticipated electric sales.&#160; However, we may not be able to hedge the entire
exposure of our operations from fuel price volatility.&#160; As of the date of this report, we have hedged
our coal requirements with coal mine operators and financial institutions to
meet our committed burn through December&nbsp;31, 2010.&#160; Historically, some of our suppliers and
buyers of fuel have not performed on their contracts and have failed to deliver
or accept fuel as specified under their contracts</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; </font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">23<a name="PB_23_002626_3020"></a></font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">To the extent our suppliers
and buyers do not meet their contractual commitments, we cannot secure adequate
fuel or sell excess fuel in a timely or cost-effective manner or we are not
hedged against price volatility, our results of operations, financial condition
and cash flows could be materially adversely affected.&#160; In addition, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is a co-owner of certain generation facilities where it is a non-operating
partner.<b>&#160; DP&amp;L</b>
does not procure or have control over the fuel for these facilities, but is
responsible for its proportionate share of the cost of fuel procured at these
facilities.&#160; Co-owner operated facilities
do not always have realized fuel costs that are equal to our co-owners&#146;
projections, and we are responsible for our proportionate share of any increase
in actual fuel costs.&#160; Pursuant to its
electric security plan, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
implemented a fuel and purchased power recovery mechanism beginning on January&nbsp;1,
2010, which will track and adjust fuel costs on a seasonal quarterly
basis.&#160; If in the future we are unable to
timely or fully recover our fuel costs, it could have a material adverse effect
on our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Commodity Trading</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We trade coal, power and
other commodities to hedge our positions in these commodities.&#160; These trades are impacted by a range of
factors, including variations in power demand, fluctuations in market prices,
market prices for alternative commodities and optimization opportunities.&#160; We have attempted to manage our commodities
trading risk exposure by establishing and enforcing risk limits and risk
management policies.&#160; Despite our
efforts, however, these risk limits and management policies may not work as
planned and fluctuating prices and other events could adversely affect our
results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160; As part of our risk management, we use a
variety of non-derivative and derivative instruments, such as swaps, futures and
forwards, to manage our market risks.&#160; In
the absence of actively quoted market prices and pricing information from
external sources, the valuation of some of these derivative instruments
involves management&#146;s judgment or use of estimates.&#160; As a result, changes in the underlying
assumptions or use of alternative valuation methods could affect the reported
fair value of some of these contracts.&#160;
We could also recognize financial losses as a result of volatility in
the market values of these contracts or if a counterparty fails to perform,
which could result in a material adverse effect on our results of operations,
financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:auto;text-align:left;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Environmental
Compliance</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our operations and
facilities (both wholly-owned and co-owned with others) are subject to numerous
and extensive federal, state and local environmental laws and regulations
relating to air quality (such as reducing NOx, SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2, </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">3</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;(sulfur trioxide) and mercury emissions and
potential future control of GHG emissions as discussed in more detail in the
next risk factor), water quality, wastewater discharge, solid waste (such as
the potential&#160; future regulation of ash
generated from coal-based generating stations), hazardous waste and health and
safety.&#160; With respect to our largest
generation station, the J.M. Stuart Station, we are also subject to continuing
compliance requirements related to NOx, SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2 </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">and particulate matter emissions under <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
consent decree with the Sierra Club.&#160;
Compliance with these laws, regulations and other requirements requires
us to expend significant funds and resources.&#160;
These expenditures have been significant in the past and we expect that
they will increase in the future. Complying with these numerous requirements
could at some point become prohibitively expensive and result in our shutting
down (temporarily or permanently) or altering the operation of our
facilities.&#160; Environmental laws and
regulations also generally require us to obtain and comply with a wide variety
of environmental licenses, permits, inspections and other approvals.&#160; If we are not able to timely obtain, maintain
or comply with all licenses, permits, inspections and approvals required to
operate our business, then our operations could be prevented, delayed or
subject to additional costs.&#160; Failure to
comply with environmental laws, regulations and other requirements may result
in the imposition of fines and penalties and the imposition of stricter
environmental standards and controls and other injunctive measures affecting
operating assets.&#160; In addition, any
alleged violation of these laws, regulations and other requirements may require
us to expend significant resources to defend against any such alleged
violations.&#160; We own a non-controlling
interest in several generating stations operated by our co-owners.&#160; As a non-controlling owner in these
generating stations, we are responsible for our pro rata share of expenditures
for complying with environmental laws, regulations and other requirements, but
have limited control over the compliance measures taken by our co-owners.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> has an
EIR in place as part of its existing rate plan structure, the last increase of
which occurs in 2010 and remains at that level through 2012.&#160; In addition, <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
electric security plan permits it to seek recovery for costs associated with
new climate change or carbon regulations.&#160;
While we expect to recover certain environmental costs and expenditures
from customers, if in the future we are unable to fully recover our costs in a
timely manner it could have a material adverse effect on our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160;
In addition, if we were found not to be in compliance with these
environmental laws, regulations or requirements, any penalties that would apply
would likely not be recoverable from customers and could have a material
adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and cash
flows.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">24<a name="PB_24_002639_7748"></a></font></p>
