<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Regulation
of GHGs</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">There is a growing
concern nationally and internationally among regulators, investors and others
concerning global climate change and the contribution of emissions of GHG,
including most significantly, CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&#160; This concern has led to increased interest in
legislation and action at the federal and state levels, as well as litigation,
relating to GHG emissions, including a recent declaration by the USEPA that
GHGs pose a danger to the public health that may allow the USEPA to directly
regulate greenhouse emissions.&#160; There
have been various GHG legislative proposals introduced in Congress (with one
bill passed by the House of Representatives in 2009) and there is growing
consensus that some form of legislation of GHG emissions will be approved at
the federal level that could result in substantial additional costs in the form
of taxes or emission allowances.&#160;
Approximately 99% of the energy we produce is generated by coal.&#160; If legislation or regulations are passed at
the federal or state levels imposing mandatory reductions of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and other GHGs
on generation facilities, we could be required to make large additional capital
investments.&#160; Legislation and regulations
could also impair the value of our generation stations or make some of these
stations uneconomical to maintain or operate and it could raise uncertainty
about the future viability of fossil fuels, particularly coal, as an energy
source for new and existing generation stations.&#160; Although <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
permitted under its current electric security plan to seek recovery of costs
associated with new climate change or carbon regulations, our inability to
fully or timely recover such costs could have a material adverse effect on our
results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Sales of
Excess Emission Allowances</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DP&amp;L</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> has a program for selling excess
emission allowances.&#160; During 2009 and
2008, <b>DP&amp;L</b> sold excess emission
allowances to various counterparties realizing total net gains of $5.0 million
and $34.8 million, respectively.&#160; Sales
of excess emission allowances are impacted by a range of factors, such as
general economic conditions, fluctuations in market demand, availability of
excess inventory available for sale and changes to the regulatory environment,
including the status of the USEPA&#146;s CAIR.&#160;
These factors could cause the amount of excess emission allowances we
sell to fluctuate, which could cause a material adverse effect on our results
or operations, financial condition and cash flows for any particular period.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;11, 2008,
the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued
a decision that vacated the CAIR and its associated Federal Implementation
Plan. This decision remanded these issues back to the USEPA.&#160; The USEPA issued CAIR on March&nbsp;10, 2005
to regulate certain upwind states with respect to fine particulate matter and
ozone.&#160; CAIR created interstate trading
programs for annual NOx emission allowances and made modifications to an
existing trading program for SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;that were to take effect in 2010.&#160; The district court&#146;s decision, in part,
invalidated the new NOx</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">  </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">annual emission allowance trading program
and the modifications to the SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emission trading program and created
uncertainty regarding future NOx and SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emission reduction requirements and their
timing.&#160; On December&nbsp;23, 2008, the
court reversed part of its decision that vacated CAIR.&#160; Thus, CAIR currently remains in effect, but
the USEPA remains subject to the district court&#146;s order to revise the
program.&#160; In January&nbsp;2010, the Court
ordered the USEPA to file a response to request for a USEPA decision filed by
parties in the original case who are now seeking a Court order to require the
USEPA to issue new regulations by March&nbsp;1, 2010.&#160; We cannot at this time predict the timing or
the outcome of any new regulations relating to CAIR.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DP&amp;L</font></b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#146;s
program for selling excess emission allowances includes sales of annual NOx
emission allowances and SO</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">&#160;</font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">emission
allowances that were the subject of CAIR trading programs.&#160; Although we continue selling emission
allowances, the district court&#146;s CAIR decision has affected the emission
allowance trading market and <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
program for selling additional excess allowances.&#160; The long-term impact of the district court&#146;s
decision, and of the actions the USEPA or others will take in response to this
decision, on <b>DPL</b> and <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is not fully known at this time, but could affect the amount of excess emission
allowances we sell and thus have an adverse effect on us.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Customer Switching</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Customers
can elect to take generation service from a CRES provider offering services to
customers in <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s </b>service territory.&#160; Although retail generation service has been a
competitive service since January&nbsp;1, 2001, the competitive generation
market has not developed to date in <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
service territory to any significant degree.&#160;
As of December&nbsp;31, 2009, six unaffiliated CRES providers have been
certified by the PUCO to provide generation service to <b>DP&amp;L </b>customers.&#160; DPLER, a wholly-owned subsidiary of <b>DPL</b>,<b>  </b>is also a certified CRES provider and
accounted for 99% of the total kWh consumed by customers served by CRES
providers in <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> service
territory in 2009.&#160; Increased competition
by CRES providers in our service territory for retail generation service could
result in the loss of existing customers and increased costs to retain or
attract customers, which could have a material adverse effect on our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160;
The following are a few of the factors that could result in increased
switching by customers to CRES providers in the future:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Low
wholesale price levels could lead to existing CRES providers becoming more
active in our service territory, and new CRES providers entering our territory.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We
could also experience customer switching through &#147;governmental aggregation,&#148;
where a municipality may contract with a CRES provider to provide generation
service to the customers located within the municipal boundaries.&#160; Several communities in <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> service territory passed
ordinances during 2003-2004 allowing them to become government aggregators.&#160; To date, no aggregation program has been
implemented.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Increased
customer switching in other Ohio utility service territories could lead to new
market entrants and more aggressive measures to secure customers by CRES
providers.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Operation
and Performance of Facilities</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The operation and
performance of our generation, transmission and distribution facilities and
equipment is subject to various events and risks, such as the potential
breakdown or failure of equipment, processes or facilities, fuel supply or
transportation disruptions, the loss of cost-effective disposal options for
solid waste generated by our facilities (such as gypsum), accidents, injuries,
labor disputes or work stoppages&nbsp;by employees, operator error, acts of
terrorism or sabotage, construction delays or cost overruns, shortages of or
delays in obtaining equipment, material and labor, operational restrictions
resulting from environmental limitations and governmental interventions,
performance below expected levels, weather-related and other natural
disruptions, vandalism, events occurring on the systems of third parties that
interconnect to and affect our system and the increased costs and enhanced
risks associated with our aging generation units.&#160; Our results of operations, financial
condition and cash flows could be adversely affected due to the happening or
continuation of these events.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Operation of our owned
and co-owned generating stations below expected capacity levels, or unplanned
outages at these stations, could cause reduced energy output and efficiency
levels and likely result in lost revenues and increased expenses that could
have a material adverse effect on our results of operations, financial
condition and cash flows.&#160; In particular,
since over 50% of our base-load generation is derived from co-owned generation
stations operated by our co-owners, poor operational performance by our
co-owners, misalignment of co-owners&#146; interests or lack of control over costs
(such as fuel costs) incurred at these stations could have an adverse effect on
us.&#160; We have constructed and placed into
service FGD facilities at most of our base-load generating stations.&#160; If there is significant operational failure
of the FGD equipment at the generating stations, we may not be able to meet
emission requirements at some of our generating stations or, at other stations,
it may require us to burn more expensive cleaner coal or utilize emission
allowances.&#160; These events could result in
a substantial increase in our operating costs.&#160;
Depending on the degree, nature, extent, or willfulness of any failure
to comply with environmental requirements, including those imposed by the
Consent Decree, such non-compliance could result in the imposition of penalties
or the shutting down of the affected generating stations, which could have a
material adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and
cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Asbestos and other
regulated substances are, and may continue to be, present at our facilities
where suitable alternative materials are not available.&#160; Although we believe that any asbestos at our
facilities is contained and suitable, we have been named as a defendant in
pending asbestos litigation, which at this time is not material to us.&#160; The continued presence of asbestos and other
regulated substances at these facilities could result in additional litigation
being brought against us, which could have a material adverse effect on our
results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Reliability Standards</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As an owner and operator
of a bulk power transmission system, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
subject to mandatory reliability standards promulgated by the NERC and enforced
by the FERC.&#160; The standards are based on
the functions that need to be performed to ensure the bulk power system
operates reliably and is guided by reliability and market interface
principles.&#160; In addition, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is subject to new Ohio reliability standards and
targets.&#160; Compliance with reliability
standards subjects us to higher operating costs or increased capital
expenditures.&#160; While we expect to recover
costs and expenditures from customers through regulated rates, there can be no
assurance that the PUCO will approve full recovery in a timely manner.&#160; If we were found not to be in compliance with
the mandatory reliability standards, we could be subject to sanctions,
including substantial monetary penalties, which likely would not be recoverable
from customers through regulated rates and could have a material adverse effect
on our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Weather
Conditions</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Weather conditions significantly affect the demand for electric
power.&#160; In our Ohio service territory,
demand for electricity is generally greater in the summer months associated
with cooling and in the winter months associated with heating as compared to
other times of the year.&#160; Unusually mild
summers and winters could therefore have an adverse effect on our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160;
In addition, severe or unusual weather, such as hurricanes and ice or
snow storms, may cause outages and property damage that may require us to incur
additional costs that may not be insured or recoverable from customers.&#160; While <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
permitted to seek recovery of storm damage costs under its electric security
plan, if <b>DP&amp;L</b> is unable to fully recover
such costs in a timely manner, it could have a material adverse effect on our
results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Regional Transmission
Organizational Risks</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On October&nbsp;1, 2004,
in compliance with Ohio law, <b>DP&amp;L</b> turned
over control of its transmission functions and fully integrated into PJM.&nbsp;
The price at which we can sell our generation capacity and energy is now determined
through supply and demand and the behavior of market participants.&nbsp; While
we can continue to make bilateral transactions to sell our generation through a
willing-buyer and willing-seller relationship, any transactions that are not
pre-arranged are subject to market conditions at PJM.&nbsp; To the extent we
sell electricity into the power markets on a contractual basis, we are not
guaranteed any rate of return on our capital investments through mandated
rates.&#160; These sales are dependent upon
prevailing market prices, which could fluctuate substantially over relatively
short periods of time and adversely affect our results of operations, financial
condition and cash flows.<b>&#160; </b>The rules&nbsp;governing the
various regional power markets also change from time to time which could affect
our costs and revenues.&nbsp; We incur fees and costs to participate in the
RTO.&nbsp; We may be limited with respect to the price at which power may be
sold from certain generating units and we may be required to expand our transmission
system according to decisions made by the RTO rather than our internal planning
process.&nbsp; While RTO transmission rates were initially designed to be
revenue neutral, various proposals and proceedings currently taking place at
FERC may cause transmission rates to change from time to time.&nbsp; In
addition, developing rules&nbsp;associated with the allocation and methodology
of assigning costs associated with improved transmission reliability, reduced
transmission congestion and firm transmission rights may have a financial
impact on us.&nbsp; While the impact of the capacity market and other RTO
developments on us at any given time will depend on a variety of factors,
including the market behavior of various participants, our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows could be materially adversely
affected.&#160; Future capacity auction
results will be dependent not only on the overall supply and demand of
generation and load, but also by congestion and PJM&#146;s business rules&nbsp;relating
to bidding for Demand Response and Energy Efficiency resources in the
auctions.&#160; The PJM RPM base residual
auction for the 2012/2013 period cleared at a per megawatt price of $16/day for
our RTO area.&#160; Prior to this auction, the
per megawatt price for the 2011/2012 period was $110/day.&#160; We cannot predict the outcome of future
auctions, but if the current auction price is sustained or there is continued
volatility in the auction market, our results of operations, financial
condition and cash flows could be materially adversely affected.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">SB 221 includes a provision that allows
electric utilities to seek and obtain deferral and recovery of RTO related
charges.&nbsp; If in the future, however, we are unable to defer or recover all
of these cost in a timely manner, it could have a material adverse effect on
our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As members of
PJM, <b>DP&amp;L</b> and DPLE are subject to
certain additional risks including those associated with the allocation among
PJM members of losses caused by unreimbursed defaults of other participants in
PJM markets and those associated with complaint cases filed against PJM that
may seek refunds of revenues previously earned by PJM members including <b>DP&amp;L</b> and DPLE.&#160;
These amounts could be significant and have a material adverse effect on
our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">27<a name="PB_27_002734_8146"></a></font></p>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">PJM
Infrastructure Risks</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Annually, PJM performs a review of the capital additions required to
provide reliable electric transmission services throughout its territory.&#160; PJM traditionally allocated the costs of
constructing these facilities to those entities that benefited directly from
the additions. &#160;On April&nbsp;19, 2007,
the FERC issued an order that modified the traditional method of allocating
costs associated with new high voltage planned transmission facilities.&#160; FERC ordered that the cost of new
high-voltage facilities be socialized across the PJM region.&#160; The costs of the new facilities at lower
voltages will continue to be assigned to the load centers that benefit from the
new facilities.&#160; With respect to the
socialization of new high voltage facilities, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals, D.C. Circuit on March&nbsp;18,
2008 challenging the allocation method.&nbsp; The appeal was consolidated with
other appeals taken by other petitioners of the same FERC Orders and the
consolidated cases were assigned to the 7</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">th</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;Circuit.&nbsp; On August&nbsp;6, 2009, the 7</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">th</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;Circuit ruled that the FERC had failed to
provide a reasoned basis for the allocation method for new high voltage
facilities that it had approved.&nbsp; Subsequently, the 7</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:-3.0pt;">th</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;Circuit denied other petitioners&#146; rehearing
requests and remanded the case to the FERC for further proceedings. &#160;Until such time as FERC may act to approve a
change in methodology, PJM will continue to apply the allocation methodology
that had been approved by FERC in 2007. At this time, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is unable to predict the outcome of this matter.&#160; The overall impact of FERC&#146;s allocation
methodology cannot be definitively assessed at this time because not all new
planned construction is likely to happen.&#160;
The additional costs allocated to <b>DP&amp;L</b> for
new large transmission approved projects were immaterial in 2009 and are not
expected to be material in 2010, but could rise to approximately $12 million or
more annually by 2012.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b> sought and obtained PUCO authority to defer and
recover costs associated with these new high-voltage transmission projects
through retail rates. However, if in the future we are unable to defer or
recover these costs, it could have a material adverse effect on our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Credit
and Capital Markets</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">From time to time we rely on access to the
credit and capital markets to fund certain of our operational and capital
costs.&#160; These capital and credit markets
have experienced extreme volatility and disruption and the ability of
corporations to obtain funds through the issuance of debt or equity has been
negatively impacted.&#160; Disruptions in the
credit and capital markets make it harder and more expensive to obtain funding
for our business.&#160; Access to funds under
our existing financing arrangements is also dependent on the ability of our
counterparties to meet their financing commitments.&#160; Our inability to obtain financing on
reasonable terms, or at all, with creditworthy counterparties could adversely
affect our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160; If our available funding is limited or we are
forced to fund our operations at a higher cost, these conditions may require us
to curtail our business activities and increase our cost of funding, both of
which could reduce our profitability.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> variable rate debt bears interest based on a
prevailing rate that is reset weekly based on a market index that can be
affected by market demand, supply, market interest rates and other market
conditions.&#160; We also currently maintain
both cash on deposit and investments in cash equivalents that could be
adversely affected by interest rate fluctuations.&#160; In addition, select debt of <b>DPL</b> and <b>DP&amp;L</b> is
currently rated investment grade by various rating agencies.&#160; If the rating agencies were to rate <b>DPL</b> and <b>DP&amp;L</b> below investment
grade, our borrowing costs would increase, we would likely be required to pay a
higher interest rate under certain existing and future financings and our
potential pool of investors and funding sources would likely decrease.&#160; Our credit ratings also govern the collateral
provisions of certain of our contracts, and a below investment grade credit
rating by one of the rating agencies could require us to post cash collateral
under these contracts.&#160; These events
would likely reduce our liquidity and profitability and could have a material
adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and cash
flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Value and Funding of
Benefit Plan Assets</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The performance of the
capital markets affects the values of the assets that are held in trust to
satisfy future obligations under our pension and postretirement benefit
plans.&#160; These assets are subject to
market fluctuations and will yield uncertain returns, which may fall below our
projected return rates.&#160; A decline in the
market value of the pension and postretirement benefit plan assets will
increase the funding requirements under our pension and postretirement benefit
plans if the actual asset returns do not recover these declines in value in the
foreseeable future.&#160; Future pension
funding requirements, and the timing of funding payments, may also be subject
to changes in legislation.&#160; The Pension
Protection Act, enacted in August&nbsp;2006, requires underfunded pension plans
to improve their funding ratios within prescribed intervals based on the level
of their underfunding.&#160; As a result, our
required contributions to these plans may increase in the future.&#160; In addition, our pension and postretirement
benefit plan liabilities are sensitive to changes in interest rates.&#160; As interest rates decrease, the liabilities
increase, potentially increasing benefit expense and funding requirements.&#160; Further, changes in demographics, including
increased numbers of retirements or changes in life expectancy assumptions, may
also increase the funding requirements of the obligations related to the
pension and other postretirement benefit plans.&#160;
Declines in market values and increased funding requirements could have
a material adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and
cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Reliance
on Third Parties</font></u></b></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We enter into
transactions with and rely on many counterparties in connection with our
business, including for the purchase and delivery of inventory, which includes
fuel and equipment components (such as limestone for our FGD equipment), for
our capital improvements and additions and to provide professional services,
such as actuarial calculations, payroll processing and various consulting
services.&#160; If any of these counterparties
fails to perform its obligations to us or becomes unavailable, our business
plans may be materially disrupted, we may be forced to discontinue certain
operations if a cost-effective alternative is not readily available or we may
be forced to enter into alternative arrangements at then-current market prices
that may exceed our contractual prices and cause delays.&#160; These events could cause our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows to be materially adversely
affected.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Our
Stock Price May&nbsp;Fluctuate</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The market price of <b>DPL&#146;s</b> common stock has fluctuated over a relatively wide
range.&#160; Over the past three years, the
market price of our common stock has fluctuated with a low of $19.16 and a high
of $31.91.&#160; Our common stock in recent
years has experienced significant price and volume variations that have often
been unrelated to our operating performance.&#160;
Over the previous year, the global markets have increasingly been
characterized by substantially increased volatility in companies in a number of
industries and in the broader markets.&#160;
The market price of our common stock may continue to significantly
fluctuate in the future and may be affected adversely by factors such as actual
or anticipated change in our operating results, acquisition activity, changes
in financial estimates by securities analysts, general market conditions,
rumors and other factors, which factors may increase price volatility and be
exacerbated by continued disruption in the global markets at large.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-align:left;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Economic Conditions and Markets</font></u></b></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Economic pressures, as
well as changing market conditions and other factors related to physical energy
and financial trading activities, which include price, credit, liquidity,
volatility, capacity, transmission and interest rates, can have a significant
effect on our operations and the operations of our retail, industrial and
commercial customers and our suppliers.&#160;
The direction and relative strength of the global economy has been
increasingly uncertain due to softness in the real estate and mortgage markets,
volatility in fuel and other energy costs, difficulties in the financial
services sector and credit markets, increased unemployment and other
factors.&#160; Many of these factors have
disproportionately impacted our Ohio service territory.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows may be negatively affected by
sustained downturns or a sluggish economy.&#160;
Sustained downturns, recession or a sluggish economy generally affect
the markets in which we operate and negatively influence our energy
operations.&#160; A contracting, slow or
sluggish economy could reduce the demand for energy in areas in which we are
doing business.&#160; During economic
downturns, our commercial and industrial customers may see a decrease in demand
for their products, which in turn may lead to a decrease in the amount of
energy they require.&#160; In addition, our
customers&#146; ability to pay us could also be impaired, which could result in an
increase in receivables and write-offs of uncollectible accounts.&#160; Our suppliers could also be affected by the
economic downturn resulting in supply delays or unavailability.&#160; Reduced demand for our electric services,
failure by our customers to timely remit full payment owed to us and supply delays
or unavailability could have a material adverse effect on our results of
operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Warrant
Exercise</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DPL&#146;s</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> warrant holders can exercise their
warrants to purchase shares of <b>DPL</b> common
stock at their discretion until March&nbsp;12, 2012.&#160; As of the date of this report, the number of
outstanding warrants is 1.8 million.&#160; As
a result, <b>DPL</b> could be required to
issue up to 1.8 million common shares in exchange for the receipt of the
exercise price of $21.00 per share or pursuant to a cashless exercise
process.&#160; The exercise of warrants would
increase the number of common shares outstanding and increase our common share
dividend costs, thus affecting any existing guidance on EPS and adversely
affecting our financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-align:left;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Internal Controls and Information
Reporting</font></u></b></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our internal controls,
accounting policies and practices and internal information systems are designed
to enable us to capture and process transactions and information in a timely
and accurate manner in compliance with GAAP in the United States of America,
laws and regulations, taxation requirements and federal securities laws and
regulations in order to, among other things, disclose and report financial and
other information in connection with the recovery of our costs and with our
reporting requirements under federal securities, tax and other laws and
regulations and to properly process payments.&#160;
We have implemented corporate governance, internal control and
accounting policies and procedures in connection with the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of
2002 (the &#147;Act&#148;).&#160; Our internal controls
and policies have been and continue to be closely monitored by management and
our Board of Directors to ensure continued compliance with Section&nbsp;404 of
the Act.&#160; </font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Our Consolidated Financial Statements are
prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the
United States of America.&#160; The SEC, FASB
or other authoritative bodies or governmental entities may issue new
pronouncements or new interpretations of existing accounting standards that may
require us to change our accounting policies.&#160;
These changes are beyond our control, can be difficult to predict and
could materially impact how we report our results of operations, financial
condition and cash flows.&#160; We could be
required to apply a new or revised standard retroactively, which could
adversely affect our financial position.&#160;
In addition, in preparing our Consolidated Financial Statements,
management is required to make estimates and assumptions.&#160; Actual results could differ significantly
from those estimates.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The SEC has issued a roadmap for the
transition by U.S. public companies to the use of International Financial
Reporting Standards (IFRS) promulgated by the International Accounting
Standards Board. Under the SEC&#146;s proposed roadmap, we could be required to
prepare financial statements in accordance with IFRS in 2014.&#160; The SEC expects to make a determination in
2011 regarding the mandatory adoption of IFRS.&#160;
We are currently assessing the impact that this potential change would
have on our Consolidated Financial Statements and we will continue to monitor
the development of the potential implementation of IFRS.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Qualified
and Properly Motivated Workforce</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">One of the challenges we
face is to retain a skilled, efficient and cost-effective workforce while
recruiting new talent to replace losses in knowledge and skills due to
retirements.&#160; This undertaking could
require us to make additional financial commitments and incur increased costs.&#160; If we are unable to successfully attract and
retain an appropriately qualified workforce, our results of operations,
financial condition and cash flows could be materially adversely affected.&#160; In addition, we have employee compensation
plans that reward the performance of our employees.&#160; While we seek to ensure that our compensation
plans encourage acceptable levels for risk and high performance through pay
mix, performance metrics and timing, and although we have policies and
procedures in place to mitigate excessive risk-taking by employees, excessive
risk-taking by our employees to achieve performance targets could result in
events that could have a material adverse effect on our results of operations,
financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Collective
Bargaining Agreements and Employee Relations</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Over half of our
employees are represented by a collective bargaining agreement that is in
effect until October&nbsp;31, 2011.&#160;
While we believe that we maintain a satisfactory relationship with our
employees, it is possible that labor disruptions affecting some or all of our
operations could occur during the period of the bargaining agreement or at the
expiration of the collective bargaining agreement before a new agreement is
negotiated.&#160; Work stoppages&nbsp;by, or
poor relations or ineffective negotiations with, our employees could have a
material adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and
cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;text-indent:0in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Cyber
Security and Terrorism</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Man-made
problems such as computer viruses, terrorism, theft and sabotage, may disrupt
our operations and harm our operating results.&#160;
We operate in a highly regulated industry that requires the continued
operation of sophisticated information technology systems and network
infrastructure.&#160; Despite our
implementation of security measures, all of our technology systems are
vulnerable to disability, failures or unauthorized access due to hacking,
viruses, acts of war or terrorism and other causes.&#160; If our technology systems were to fail or be
breached and we were unable to recover in a timely way, we would be unable to
fulfill critical business functions and sensitive confidential and other data
could be compromised, which could have a material adverse effect on our results
of operations, financial condition and cash flows.&#160; In addition, our generation plants, fuel
storage facilities, transmission and distribution facilities may be targets of
terrorist activities that could disrupt our ability to produce or distribute
some portion of our energy products.&#160; Any
such disruption could result in a material decrease in revenues and significant
additional costs to repair and insure our assets, which could have a material
adverse effect on our results of operations, financial condition and cash
flows.&#160; The continued threat of terrorism
and heightened security and military action in response to this threat, or any
future acts of terrorism, may cause further disruptions to the economies of the
United States and other countries and create further uncertainties or otherwise
materially harm our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DPL as Holding Company</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DPL</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> is a holding company and its
investments in its subsidiaries are its primary assets.&#160; Substantially all of <b>DPL&#146;s</b>
business is conducted by its <b>DP&amp;L</b>
subsidiary.&#160; As such, <b>DPL&#146;s</b> cash flow is dependent on the operating cash flows of <b>DP&amp;L</b> and its ability to pay cash to <b>DPL</b>.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
governing documents contain certain limitations on the ability to declare and
pay dividends to <b>DPL</b> while preferred stock is
outstanding.&#160; Certain of <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> debt agreements also contain limits with respect
to the ability of <b>DP&amp;L</b> to
loan or advance funds to <b>DPL.</b>&#160; In addition, <b>DP&amp;L</b>
is regulated by the PUCO that possesses broad oversight powers to ensure that
the needs of utility customers are being met.&#160;
While we are not currently aware of any plans to do so, the PUCO could
attempt to impose restrictions on the ability of <b>DP&amp;L</b>
to pay cash to <b>DPL</b> pursuant to these broad
powers.&#160; While we do not expect any
foregoing restrictions to significantly affect <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
ability to pay funds to <b>DPL </b>in the
future, a significant limitation on <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s </b>ability
to pay dividends or loan or advance funds to <b>DPL</b>
would materially adversely affect <b>DPL&#146;s</b> results
of operations, financial condition and cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">None</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

are subject to the lien of the mortgage securing <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> First and Refunding Mortgage, dated as of October&nbsp;1,

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Item 3 - Legal Proceedings</font></b><a name="Item3LegalProceedings_215102"></a></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In the normal course of
business, we are subject to various lawsuits, actions, proceedings, claims and
other matters asserted under laws and regulations.&#160; We are also from time to time involved in
other reviews, investigations and proceedings by governmental and regulatory
agencies regarding our business, certain of which may result in adverse
judgments, settlements, fines, penalties, injunctions or other relief.&#160; We believe the amounts provided in our
Consolidated Financial Statements, as prescribed by GAAP, for these matters are
adequate in light of the probable and estimable contingencies.&#160; However, there can be no assurances that the
actual amounts required to satisfy alleged liabilities from various legal proceedings,
claims and other matters (including those matters noted below) and to comply
with applicable laws and regulations will not exceed the amounts reflected in
our Consolidated Financial Statements.&#160;
As such, costs, if any, that may be incurred in excess of those amounts
provided as of December&nbsp;31, 2009, cannot be reasonably determined.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-indent:.5in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DP&amp;L&#146;s</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> common stock is held solely by <b>DPL </b>and, as a result, is not listed for
trading on any stock exchange.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As long as <b>DP&amp;L</b> preferred stock is outstanding, <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> Amended Articles of
Incorporation contain provisions restricting the payment of cash dividends on
any of its common stock if, after giving effect to such dividend, the aggregate
of all such dividends distributed subsequent to December&nbsp;31, 1946 exceeds
the net income of <b>DP&amp;L</b>
available for dividends on its Common Stock subsequent to December&nbsp;31,
1946, plus $1.2&nbsp;million.&#160; This
dividend restriction has historically not impacted <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s </b>ability
to pay cash dividends and, as of December&nbsp;31, 2009, <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b> retained earnings of $640.3
million were all available for <b>DP&amp;L</b>
common stock dividends payable to <b>DPL.</b></font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DPL</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> paid regular quarterly cash dividends of
$0.285 and $0.275 per share on our common stock during 2009 and 2008,
respectively.&#160; The annualized dividend
rate was $1.14 per share in 2009 and $1.10 per share in 2008.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On December&nbsp;9, 2009,
<b>DPL&#146;s </b>Board of Directors authorized a
quarterly dividend rate increase of approximately 6%, increasing the quarterly
dividend per <b>DPL</b> common share from $0.2850 to
$0.3025, effective with the next dividend declaration.&#160; If this dividend rate were maintained, the
annualized dividend would increase from $1.14 per share to $1.21 per share. &#160;Additional information concerning dividends
paid on <b>DPL</b> common stock is set
forth under Selected Quarterly Information in Item 8 &#151; Financial Statements and
Supplementary Data.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Information regarding <b>DPL&#146;s </b>equity compensation plans as of December&nbsp;31, 2009
is disclosed in Item&nbsp;12 &#151; Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners
and Management and Related Stockholder Matters, which incorporates such
information by reference from <b>DPL&#146;s</b> proxy
statement for the 2010 Annual Meeting of Shareholders.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt 13.5pt;text-indent:-13.5pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">(4)&nbsp;On October&nbsp;28, 2009, the <b>DPL</b>
Board of Directors approved, and <b>DPL </b>publicly
announced, a Stock Repurchase Program under which <b>DPL </b>may
use proceeds from the exercise of warrants to repurchase warrants or <b>DPL </b>common stock from time to time in the open market,
through private transactions or otherwise.&#160;
Through December&nbsp;31, 2009, the amount of such proceeds available to
be used under the Stock Repurchase Program approximated $68.3 million, of which
$64.4 million was used during the quarter ended December&nbsp;31, 2009 to
purchase approximately 2.4 million shares at an average per share price of
$26.96.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the
amount still available that could be used to repurchase stock under the Stock
Repurchase Program is approximately $3.9 million but could be higher if
additional warrants are exercised for cash in the future.&#160; The Stock Repurchase Program will run through
June&nbsp;30, 2012, which is approximately three months after the end of the
warrant exercise period.</font></i></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The graph below matches <b>DPL&#146;s</b> cumulative 5-year total shareholder return on common
stock with the cumulative total returns of the Dow Jones US Industrial Average
index, the S&amp;P Utilities index and the S&amp;P Electric Utilities index.
The graph tracks the performance of a $1,000 investment in our common stock and
in each index (with the reinvestment of all dividends) from December&nbsp;31,
2004 to December&nbsp;31, 2009.</font></p>

facilities resulting in a $44.2 million ($71 million pre-tax) impairment
charge.&#160; The sale was finalized in April&nbsp;2007.&#160; During 2006, <b>DPL</b>
recorded a $37.3 million ($61.2 million pre-tax) charge for early redemption of
debt.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
recorded a $2.5 million ($4.1 million pre-tax) charge for early redemption of
debt in 2006.&#160; In May&nbsp;2007, <b>DPL</b> settled the litigation with former executives resulting
in a $19.7 million ($31 million pre-tax) gain.&#160;
In April&nbsp;2007, <b>DPL </b>also
recouped legal costs associated with the litigation with the former executives
from one of its insurers resulting in a $9.2 million ($14.5 million pre-tax)
gain.&#160; In 2008, <b>DPL</b>
sold coal and excess emission allowances to various counterparties, realizing
net gains of $58.2 million ($83.4 million pre-tax) and $24.3 million ($34.8
million pre-tax), respectively.&#160; Also, in
June&nbsp;2008, <b>DPL</b> entered into a $42 million tax
settlement with ODT resulting in a recorded income tax benefit of $8.5 million.</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Item 7 - Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial
Condition and Results of Operations</font></b><a name="Item7ManagementsDiscussionAndAnal_221508"></a></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

combined filing of <b>DPL Inc. (DPL)</b>
and <b>The Dayton Power and Light Company</b>  <b>(DP&amp;L).&#160; DP&amp;L </b>is
the principal subsidiary of <b>DPL </b>providing

respectively and altogether, unless the context indicates otherwise.&#160; Discussions or areas of this report that
apply only to <b>DPL</b> or <b>DP&amp;L</b>
will clearly be noted in the section.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The following discussion
should be read in conjunction with the accompanying Consolidated Financial
Statements and related footnotes included in Item 8 &#150; Financial Statements and
Supplementary Data.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">BUSINESS OVERVIEW</font></b></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DPL</font></b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> is a regional electric energy and
utility company and through its principal subsidiary <b>DP&amp;L,</b>
is primarily engaged in the generation, transmission and distribution of
electricity in West Central Ohio.&#160; <b>DPL </b>and <b>DP&amp;L</b> strive
to achieve disciplined growth in energy margins while limiting volatility in
both cash flows and earnings and to achieve stable, long-term growth through
efficient operations and strong customer and regulatory relations.&#160; More specifically, <b>DPL </b>and<b> DP&amp;L&#146;s </b>strategy is to match energy supply with load or
customer demand, maximizing profits while effectively managing exposure to
movements in energy and fuel prices and utilizing the transmission and
distribution assets that transfer electricity at the most efficient cost while
maintaining the highest level of customer service and reliability.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We operate and manage
generation assets and are exposed to a number of risks.&#160; These risks include but are not limited to
electricity wholesale price risk, fuel supply and price risk and power plant
performance.&#160; We attempt to manage these
risks through various means.&#160; For instance,
we operate a portfolio of wholly-owned and jointly-owned generation assets that
is diversified as to coal source, cost structure and operating
characteristics.&#160; We are focused on the
operating efficiency of these power plants and maintaining their availability.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">36<a name="PB_36_004105_2983"></a></font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="left"></div>

<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table
of Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">We<b>  </b>operate
and manage<b>  </b>transmission and distribution assets
in a rate-regulated environment.&#160; Accordingly,
this subjects us to regulatory risk in terms of the costs that we may recover
and the investment returns that we may collect in customer rates.&#160; We are focused on delivering electricity and
maintaining high standards of customer service and reliability in a
cost-effective manner.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As we look forward, there
are a number of issues that we believe may have a significant impact on our
business and operations described above.&#160;
The following issues mentioned below are not meant to be exhaustive but to
provide insight to matters that have or are likely to have an effect on our
industry and business:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT</font></u></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Emissions &#150; Climate Change
Legislation</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">There is a growing
concern nationally and internationally about global climate change and the
contribution of emissions of GHGs, including most significantly, CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;This concern has led to increased
interest in legislation at the federal level, actions at the state level as
well as litigation relating to GHG emissions.&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2007, a U.S.
Supreme Court decision upheld that the USEPA has the authority to regulate CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emissions from
motor vehicles under the CAA.&nbsp;&nbsp;In April&nbsp;2009, the USEPA issued a
proposed endangerment finding under the CAA, which was finalized and published December&nbsp;15,
2009.&#160; The proposed finding determined
that CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and other GHGs from motor vehicles threaten
the health and welfare of future generations by contributing to climate
change.&#160; It is anticipated that this
ruling will lead to the regulation of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and other GHGs from electric generating units
and other stationary sources of these emissions.&#160; In June&nbsp;2009, the U.S. House of
Representatives passed H.R. 2454, the American Clean Energy and Security Act
(ACES).&#160; This proposed legislation
targets a reduction in the emission of GHGs from large sources by 80% in 2050
through an economy-wide cap and trade program.&#160;
ACES also includes energy efficiency and renewable energy
initiatives.&#160; Increased pressure for CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emissions
reduction is also coming from investor organizations and the international
community.&#160; Environmental advocacy groups
are also focusing considerable attention on CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emissions from power generation facilities and
their potential role in climate change.&#160; Approximately
99% of the energy we produce is generated by coal.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s</b>
share of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;emissions at generating stations we own and
co-own is approximately 16 million tons annually.&#160; If legislation or regulations are passed at
the federal or state levels that impose mandatory reductions of CO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;and other GHGs
on generation facilities, the cost to<b> DPL</b>
and<b> DP&amp;L</b> of such reductions
could be material.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">&#183;</font></b><b><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;font-weight:bold;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font></b><b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">SB 221 Requirements</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">SB
221 and the implementation rules&nbsp;contain targets relating to advanced
energy portfolio standards, renewable energy, demand reduction and energy
efficiency standards.&#160; The standards
require that, by the year 2025, 25% of the total number of kWh of electricity
sold by the utility to retail electric consumers must come from alternative
energy resources, which include &#147;advanced energy resources&#148; such as distributed
generation, clean coal, advanced nuclear, energy efficiency and fuel cell
technology; and &#147;renewable energy resources&#148; such as solar, hydro, wind,
geothermal and biomass.&#160; At least half of
the 25% must be generated from renewable energy resources, including 0.5% from
solar energy.&#160; The renewable energy
portfolio, energy efficiency and demand reduction standards began in 2009 with
increases in required percentages each year.&#160;
The annual targets for energy efficiency and peak demand reductions
began in 2009 with annual increases.&#160;
Energy efficiency programs are to save 22.3% by 2025 and peak demand
reductions are expected to reach 7.75% by 2018 compared to a baseline energy
usage.&#160; If any targets are not met,
compliance penalties will apply, unless the PUCO makes certain findings that
would excuse performance.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">SB
221 also contains provisions for determining whether an electric utility has
significantly excessive earnings.&#160; On September&nbsp;9,
2009, the PUCO issued an entry establishing a significantly excessive earnings
test (SEET) proceeding.&#160; A workshop was
held at the Commission offices on October&nbsp;5, 2009 to allow interested
parties to present concerns and discuss issues related to the methodology.&#160; On November&nbsp;18, 2009 the PUCO Staff
issued its recommendations to the Commission.&#160;
Staff recommendations provided that off-system or wholesale sales should
be included in the calculation, and that some threshold should be established
based on a group of comparable companies that would determine if the utility
had significantly excessive earnings in a given year.&#160; <b>DP&amp;L</b>
filed its comments and reply comments along with other interested parties.&#160; Although <b>DP&amp;L&#146;s
</b>Stipulation provides that the SEET does not apply to <b>DP&amp;L</b> until 2013 based on 2012 earnings
results, <b>DP&amp;L</b> is actively
participating in this proceeding.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><b><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">CAIR decision by the U.S. Court
of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;11, 2008,
the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued
a decision that vacated the USEPA CAIR and its associated Federal Implementation
Plan. This decision remanded these issues back to the USEPA.&#160; The USEPA issued CAIR on March&nbsp;10, 2005
to regulate certain upwind states with respect to fine particulate matter and
ozone.&#160; CAIR created interstate trading
programs for annual NOx emission allowances and made modifications to an
existing trading program for SO</font><font size="1" style="font-size:6.5pt;position:relative;top:1.0pt;">2</font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160;that were to take effect in 2010.&#160; </font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">37<a name="PB_37_004105_6228"></a></font></p>

<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="left"></div>
